summary: Work with a start and an end that makes a change, then hands what it built to the people who will run it. One person leads it, with one budget.
example: Quality Check Rollout, which gets every depot checking deliveries against one standard, then hands the checks to the Quality Check Service.

results framework.summary: A project's plan in one table: what it delivers, what that changes, how each is measured, and what must be true for it to work.
results framework.example: Quality Check Rollout: a training pack and a results view, so every depot checks deliveries against one standard, measured by the quality pass rate.

component.summary: One part of a bigger project, with the same person in charge and the same budget. A part with its own leader or budget is a separate project.
component.example: Depot staff training, run as one part of the Quality Check Rollout, with the same person in charge and budget.

definition: Work that ends. One team runs it, with one sponsor (the person accountable for it) and one budget. A project produces deliverables; the benefits come later, once they are in use, so every project names the ongoing service (operation) that takes them over. A project has one objective: the change it exists to make. It serves outcomes in your strategy, and may list other projects as its components, pieces of work it depends on, each with an objective of its own. It is not an operation, which has no end date; not a programme, which groups several projects towards one change; not a goal; and not a deliverable. You fill it in over three phases: Initiation, Closure and Handover.

cues.project: a one-off job to build, set up, replace, train or roll out something

/metadata/name.guide: A short name for the project. Name it for the change it makes, not for the service that will run the result.
good: Quality Check Rollout

poor.why: That is the service that takes over the result. Name the project for the change it makes.
Says when the work happens, not what it changes.

/spec/alignment/programmes.guide: The programmes this project belongs to. If this project is part of a bigger project, leave it empty; it belongs to that project's programmes.

/spec/alignment/partOf.guide: The bigger project this one is part of, if any. Choose one only if both have the same sponsor and budget. A part cannot have parts of its own.

/spec/alignment/goals.guide: The outcomes in your strategy this project serves. Choose outcomes, not goals or objectives. If no outcome fits, add one first under its objective.

/spec/team.guide: The team that runs the project. Its members can edit it. Choose a team, not a person or a role.
good: quality-team

/spec/summary/beneficiaries.guide: The groups of people who benefit from this project, directly or indirectly. Name the groups only, with no counts or targets.

/spec/summary/beneficiaries/-/group.guide: A group of people who benefit. Include people who benefit indirectly, not only those the project serves directly.
good: delivering-members
retail-partners
depot-staff

poor.why: Too broad. Name the groups who feel the problem.

/spec/summary/problems.guide: The problems this project solves. For each, say who feels it, what is going wrong now and why, and how things will be once it is solved. Put the main problem first.

/spec/summary/problems/-/groups.guide: The groups who feel this problem.

/spec/summary/problems/-/problem/situati.guide: What is going wrong for the affected groups now. Describe the problem, not a missing solution.
good: learn of a failed delivery a season late
are told a different answer each time they ask what a passing delivery looks like

poor.text: There is no quality check tool at intake.
poor.why: Names a missing solution. Say what the groups cannot do.
Too vague. Say which group is affected and what they cannot do.

/spec/summary/problems/-/problem/cause.guide: What you think lies behind the problem. It is a potential cause, to be tested, not a proven one.
good: checks happen after dispatch and the produce has already left the depot
each depot keeps its own checklist and none of them agree

poor.text: Lack of training, old scanners, poor roads and late payments.
poor.why: Four causes at once. Name the one this project fixes, and add the others as separate problems or risks.

/spec/summary/problems/-/change/what.guide: How things will be once the problem is solved. Describe the result, not the work.
good: Every delivery is checked at intake against one published standard
One published standard is what a check is run against

poor.text: Train depot staff and roll out the check.
poor.why: Describes the work, not the result. List the work under deliverables.

/spec/summary/problems/-/change/gain.guide: What the affected groups will be able to do that they cannot do today. Optional.
good: learn of a failure the same day and can rework it
give the same answer whoever asks

poor.why: Nobody can see this. Say what they will be able to do.

/spec/summary/problems/-/gaps.guide: The gaps this problem relates to, chosen from your gaps, and which segments of each gap the project reaches. A segment is one group or place a gap is split into. If a gap is not listed yet, add it first.

/spec/summary/problems/-/gaps/-/gap.guide: A gap, chosen from your gaps.
good: faults-found-after-dispatch

/spec/summary/problems/-/gaps/-/segments.guide: The segments of the gap this project reaches. A project that starts at two depots reaches those two depots, not the whole gap. If the gap gets new segments later, choose again.

/spec/mandate.guide: What gives you permission to do this project: a decision, policy, law, regulation, contract, business case or request. Give each one's reference and date.

/spec/mandate/-/title.guide: The document's title, as written on it.
good: Approval to pilot delivery quality checks
Produce quality standard

poor.why: Not a title. Give the decision's real title and its reference.

/spec/mandate/-/reference.guide: The identifier the issuer gives it.
good: POL-QUALITY-02

/spec/mandate/-/issuer.guide: The board, committee or role that issued it, chosen from your resources. If it is not listed, add it to your resources first.
good: Steering Committee, chosen from your resources
Sponsor, one of this project's roles

poor.why: Choose the Steering Committee from your resources instead of typing its name.

/spec/mandate/-/issuedBy.guide: The body that issued it, typed in, if it is not one of your resources, such as a government, a regulator or a funder.
good: Cooperative Board

/spec/summary/scopeIn.guide: What the project covers, one line each. Say what is included, not how it will be done.
good: Checking every delivery at intake
Training depot staff to run the quality check tool

poor.why: Too broad to tell what is in or out.

/spec/summary/scopeOut.guide: What people might expect the work to do that it will not, one short line each, with the reason where it helps.
good: Checking produce already sold to retailers
Building a new digital quality check tool

poor.why: Adds nothing. Name what people might expect the project to include.

/spec/objectives.guide: The change this project makes and how, as one or more objectives. Each has one to three key results that measure the change, not the effort. Put numbers in the key results.

/spec/objectives/-/objective.guide: The change and how you will make it, such as: Catch faults at intake by checking every delivery. Put targets in the key results.
good: Catch faults at intake by checking every delivery against one standard
Standardise depot checks by training every checker against one published standard

poor.text: Improve delivery quality across the depots.
poor.why: Says what changes but not how. Add "by" and how you will do it.

poor.text: Deliver a depot staff training pack and a quality results view.
poor.why: Those are deliverables, the outputs. The objective is the change they are for.

poor.text: Catch 85% of faults at intake by checking every delivery.
poor.why: The 85% is a target and belongs in a key result; the objective says the change.

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults.guide: One to three measures that show the objective was met. For each, give today's figure, a target with a date, which way it should move, its unit if it has one, and where the figure comes from.

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults/-/metric.guide: What you count, said exactly. Count the result, not the activity.
good: the share of faults found at intake rather than by a buyer
hours between a failed check and the depot knowing

poor.why: Counts activity, not the change. Checks can all happen and catch nothing.
Not countable as written: quality of what, measured how?

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults/-/kind.guide: What sort of number this is: percent, count, money, ratio or duration. A count, money or duration needs a unit; a percent or ratio takes none.

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults/-/unit.guide: The unit for a count, money or duration, such as hours or USD. Leave it empty for a percent or a ratio.

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults/-/directio.guide: Which way the figure should move: increase, decrease, reach or maintain.

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults/-/baseline.guide: Today's figure and the month it was measured. If you do not know it yet, say why and when you will.

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults/-/target.guide: The figure to reach and the month to reach it by.

/spec/objectives/-/keyResults/-/source.guide: Where the figure comes from, chosen from your data sources. If figures are typed in by hand, or how they are collected is not decided, say how they will get in.
good: quality-check-tool

/spec/kpis.guide: The ongoing measures (KPIs) this project moves, each with the reason. Several projects can move the same KPI.

/spec/kpis/-/reason.guide: How this project moves this KPI.
good: The published standard is what the pass rate counts.

poor.why: Too vague. Say how the project moves the figure.

/spec/resources.guide: The roles the project needs and, if known, who or what fills each one. Name roles, not people. Every project needs a sponsor and a project manager; a service owner takes over the result. People who are affected but have no role go on the stakeholder map.

/spec/resources/-/role.guide: The role: sponsor, project manager, team member, user representative, technical lead, data owner, data steward, data custodian, project support or service owner.

/spec/resources/-/resource.guide: Who or what fills this role, chosen from your resources: a role, unit, outside organisation, system or facility. Leave it empty if you do not know yet.
good: depot-network
depot-supervisor
operations-lead

poor.why: A person, not a role. Name the role the person fills.
That is the role. Name who or what fills it.

/spec/resources/-/note.guide: Anything else about this role on this project.
good: Half a day a week during the pilot

/spec/funding.guide: The money the project uses, one line per currency: the amount, the currency, the budget it comes from, and whether it is approved, requested or unfunded. If a cost is not worked out yet, add it as an issue under Risks instead.

poor.text: A line with no amount, for field costs still being worked out
poor.why: Every funding line needs an amount. Add a cost not yet worked out as an issue under Risks, and raise it with whoever decides funding.

/spec/funding/-/amount.guide: The amount on this line, in its currency, as approved or requested.

/spec/funding/-/source.guide: The budget this money comes from, chosen from your funding sources. If no budget is found yet, leave it empty and set the status to unfunded or requested.
good: operating-budget

poor.why: A budget is a funding source, not a resource. Add it under funding sources.

/spec/funding/-/status.guide: Whether the money is approved, requested or unfunded. Unfunded means nobody has found the money yet.

/spec/deliverables.guide: What the project produces, each with the test it must pass and who checks it. A deliverable is something you can hand over, not an activity or a change.

/spec/deliverables/-/name.guide: The output as a noun, short enough to scan.
good: Depot staff training pack
Quality results view

poor.why: An activity. Name what it produces, such as a training pack.
A change, not an output. That belongs in an objective or a success criterion.

/spec/deliverables/-/description.guide: What the output contains, in one sentence. Optional.
good: Slides, a facilitator guide and practice materials for running the quality check tool.

/spec/deliverables/-/acceptance.guide: Who checks this deliverable and what they confirm, one for each part that needs sign-off.

/spec/deliverables/-/acceptance/-/by.guide: The role that checks this, chosen from the project's roles. If it is missing, add it under Resources first.

/spec/deliverables/-/acceptance/-/outcom.guide: What that role checks, as a test that passes or fails.
good: confirms the practice materials match the published standard
confirms the view matches the underlying spreadsheet

poor.why: Not a test. Say what is checked.

/spec/deliverables/-/tasks.guide: The tasks that produce this deliverable, as names in any order. Set dates and order in your planning tool. Optional.

/spec/deliverables/-/tasks/-/name.guide: A task that produces part of this deliverable, starting with a verb.
good: Prepare the facilitator guide
Record attendance and questions

poor.why: A date, not a task. Set dates in your planning tool.
Produces no part of this deliverable. Leave it out, or add the deliverable it belongs to.

/spec/deliverables/-/tasks/-/role.guide: The role that does this task, chosen from the project's roles. Leave it empty if you do not know yet.

/spec/deliverables/-/tasks/-/note.guide: Anything the planner should know, in one sentence. Optional.

/spec/successCriteria.guide: What must be true for the project to count as a success, not just finished. For each, say what must be true, what kind of success it is, the level to reach, where it is measured and how often, who tracks it, who signs it off, and when it is checked.

/spec/successCriteria/-/statement.guide: What must be true, clear enough for someone else to check. Put the level to reach in the standard.
good: Faults are found at intake rather than by a buyer.
Every depot runs the check unaided.
The data protection review of member delivery records is complete with no open actions.

poor.text: The project is delivered on time.
poor.why: Finishing is not the same as succeeding. Say what must be true. For a schedule goal, choose efficiency and set the date to meet.
That is a deliverable's acceptance, not success. Say what is true once the pack is in use.

poor.text: Depot staff training delivered on 2 September with attendance recorded.
poor.why: That is the training pack's acceptance test. Say what is true once the training is used, such as staff running the check unaided.

/spec/successCriteria/-/metric.guide: What kind of success this measures: efficiency, impact on the customer, impact on the team, business success, preparation for the future, or compliance (a requirement that is met or not).

/spec/successCriteria/-/standard.guide: The level to reach. Leave it empty for compliance.
good: at least 85 percent
every depot, every season

poor.why: Too vague to pass or fail.

/spec/successCriteria/-/source.guide: Where the figure comes from, chosen from your data sources. Leave it empty for compliance and efficiency.

/spec/successCriteria/-/cycle.guide: How often it is measured, chosen from your reporting cycles. Only needed if it is checked after handover.
good: seasonal-cycle

/spec/successCriteria/-/owner.guide: The role that keeps the measurement up to date, from the roles in Resources.

/spec/successCriteria/-/confirmedBy.guide: The role or governance body that decides whether this was met. Usually the sponsor, or the service owner for a criterion read after handover.

/spec/successCriteria/-/from.guide: The deliverables that make this true, if any.

/spec/successCriteria/-/assumes.guide: What must be true for the deliverables to make this happen. Choose an assumption, or add one first.

/spec/successCriteria/-/when.guide: When it is checked: at closure, when the deliverables are accepted; at handover, when the service takes over; or after handover, at each review.

/spec/timeline/phases.guide: The phases in order, each with a name and a length in months. Cartograph works out the end month.

/spec/timeline/phases/-/name.guide: What happens in the phase, in a few words.
good: Pilot at two depots
Rollout to every depot

poor.why: Say what happens in this phase.

/spec/data/consumes.guide: The data this project uses but does not change, with why and how it reaches the project.

/spec/data/consumes/-/purpose.guide: What the project uses the data for, in one sentence.
good: Identify members with deliveries due for a check this season.

poor.why: Says nothing about what the data is for.

/spec/data/consumes/-/handoff.guide: How the data reaches the project: an automatic feed, a file transfer, a shared database, manual re-entry or paper.

/spec/data/produces.guide: The data this project creates or adds to: where it is stored, why, how often, and whether it includes personal data.

/spec/data/produces/-/sink.guide: Where this data is stored afterwards. If the project builds a new data source, choose that one.

/spec/data/produces/-/purpose.guide: What the output is for, in one sentence.
good: Showing which depots are catching faults at intake rather than after dispatch.

/spec/data/produces/-/personalData.guide: Whether this data includes personal data. None: nothing in it identifies a person. Personal: it names or can identify people. Sensitive: it is about health, children, beliefs or another special category.

/spec/risks.guide: Risks (what might go wrong), issues (what is already going wrong), dependencies (what the project waits on, or what waits on it) and constraints (fixed limits). Add assumptions separately.

/spec/risks/-/description.guide: What could happen or has happened, and what it would do, in one sentence.
good: The board must approve extending the check beyond the two pilot depots.
Some quality check forms arrive at the depot office after the season closes.

poor.why: A topic, not a risk: say what might happen to it and what that would do.

poor.text: Depots release staff for training during the season.
poor.why: An assumption, not a risk. Add it as an assumption and link it to the success criterion that depends on it.

/spec/risks/-/mitigation.guide: What is done to make it less likely or less harmful, in one sentence.
good: Put the pilot's results to the board one month before rollout starts.

poor.why: Watching is not acting; say what is done and when.

/spec/risks/-/owner.guide: The role that watches this risk and acts on it day to day, chosen from the project's roles. Name one for every high-impact risk; the project manager owns the rest.
good: delivery-lead
quality-reviewer

poor.why: A person, not a role. Name the role the person fills.
The sponsor is who you go to when a risk gets too big. The owner manages it day to day.

/spec/risks/-/depends/direction.guide: Whether this project waits on the other side, or the other side waits on this project. Record it on one side only.

/spec/risks/-/depends/on.guide: What this project waits on, or what waits on it: another project, a data source, another record in Cartograph, or something outside Cartograph typed in.

/spec/risks/-/depends/needBy.guide: The phase by which the dependency must be done.

/spec/risks/-/escalate/to.guide: Whose decision is needed: usually the sponsor or a board.

/spec/risks/-/escalate/reason.guide: The decision that is needed, and why the project cannot make it.
good: Late forms are already delaying quality reporting to the board this season.

/spec/operation.guide: The ongoing service (operation) that runs the result once the project ends. Its service owner takes it over. If the service does not exist yet, add it as a planned operation first.
good: quality-check-service

/spec/notes.guide: Anything else people should know about this project.

/spec/alignment/portfolios.guide: The portfolios that select and fund this project, if any. A project may sit in a portfolio and a programme at once.

/spec/summary/about.guide: What this project is about, as you would tell a colleague. Cartograph uses it to suggest related outcomes, programmes and KPIs.
good: Train depot staff to apply one quality checklist the same way at every depot.

poor.why: Too vague. Say what the project does, and where.

/spec/summary/idea.guide: Your idea, as you first wrote it. Later steps suggest parts of it as answers.

/spec/escalationRoute.guide: Who decides when a problem cannot be solved within the project, in order, nearest first. Choose boards and roles from your resources; type in bodies outside Cartograph, such as a government.
good: Project board, then steering committee, then the national government

StakeholderMap:/spec/scope.ask: Who can affect this project or is affected by it, and for each, how much influence and how much interest do they have?
StakeholderMap:/spec/scope.ifNone: Start a stakeholder map for this project. Choose each stakeholder from your resources, adding any that are missing, and leave the scores blank until you know them.

checks.goals-aligned: Choose at least one outcome this project serves, or make it part of a bigger project that does.
checks.goals-functional-level: Align to outcomes only, not to a goal or an objective.
checks.goals-programme-membership: Choose at least one outcome that each of this project's programmes also serves.
checks.aim-mandate: Name the decision, policy, law, contract, business case or request that authorises the work.
checks.aim-problem-change: For every problem, say what is wrong now and what will change.
checks.aim-problem-groups: Name the beneficiary groups that feel each problem.
checks.scope-in: Add at least one line saying what the work covers.
checks.deliverables-acceptance: Give every deliverable at least one acceptance criterion.
checks.deliverables-verifier: Name the role that verifies every acceptance criterion.
checks.beneficiaries-named: Name at least one beneficiary group.
checks.timeline-start-phases: Set a start month and at least one phase.
checks.goals-objective: Write the project's one objective: the change it exists to make. A second change is a key result of it, or a project of its own listed as a component.
checks.goals-key-results-count: Give every objective one to three key results.
checks.goals-key-results-baseline: Give every key result today's figure with its date, or say why it is not known yet.
checks.goals-key-results-target: Give every key result a dated target.
checks.goals-key-results-source: Name the data source every key result is read from.
checks.measures-kpis: Name at least one indicator the project moves, with the reason.
checks.components-add-up: A project with parts needs a key result that its parts add up to.
checks.components-parent: Choose a different bigger project; a project cannot be part of itself.
checks.components-one-level: Choose the top project instead; a part cannot have parts of its own.
checks.components-programmes: Remove the programmes; this project belongs to its bigger project's programmes.
checks.components-one-sponsor: Use the bigger project's sponsor and budget, or make this a separate project and group the two in a programme.
checks.resources-funding: Add a funding line, even an unfunded one.
checks.resources-sponsor-lead: Name a sponsor and a project manager in Resources; a part of a bigger project needs only a project manager.
checks.resources-mapped: Choose who or what fills each role, if you know.
checks.data-personal-data: Say whether every output holds personal data.
checks.data-sink: Name the data source every output lands in.
checks.data-handoff: Replace manual re-entry with a feed, a file transfer or a shared database where you can, or note why not.
checks.data-capture-decided: Decide how figures are collected for each data source a target comes from. Set it on the data source.
checks.data-capture-turnaround: Use a data source that gets figures in fast enough for this target, or have this project speed it up.
checks.risks-owned: Name the role that owns every high-impact risk.
checks.risks-escalated: Flag a risk for escalation when it needs a decision above the project, and name whose.
checks.risks-dependency-edges: Give every dependency its direction and the other end.
checks.risks-dependency-cycle: Break the loop: one end of it must not wait on the other.
checks.risks-dependency-schedule: Move the needed-by phase, or agree an earlier finish with the other end.
checks.success-criteria: Add at least one success criterion.
checks.success-measured: Give every measured criterion a level to reach and a data source, and a reporting cycle if it is checked after handover. Efficiency needs no data source.
checks.success-owner: Name the role that tracks every criterion.
checks.closing-criteria: Give every deliverable a test it is accepted against.
checks.landing-operation: Name the operation the result is handed over to, or a new one.
checks.landing-service-funding: On the planned service, name the budget that pays to run it and the amount per month or year.
checks.landing-criteria: Add a success criterion that falls due at handover or after it.
checks.landing-owner: Name a service owner in Resources to accept the handover.
checks.measures-kpis-once: Name each KPI once, with one reason; merge the reasons if it was named twice.
checks.risks-placed: Give every risk an impact and a likelihood.
checks.compliance-as-criteria: Record each compliance line as a success criterion with metric compliance, naming the role that confirms it; then remove the line.

for.question: Who is it for?
for.cue: says who the work is for or who benefits

change.question: What will be different afterwards?
change.cue: says what will be different afterwards

deliver.question: What will it build or produce?
deliver.cue: says what the work will build or produce

when.question: When does it happen?
when.cue: says when the work happens or how long it takes

success.question: How will you know it worked?
success.cue: says how success will be measured or judged

handover.question: Who will run the result?
handover.cue: says who will run or keep the result going afterwards
